Thus the unshaded area is 75−(11+11+7+10)=36 square units. This is a valid application of composite-area addition and subtraction, supported by rectangle areas.

audits.mathematicalReason: Under the usual fair, independent-spin interpretation, the first wheel has odd probability 3/4 and even probability 1/4; the second has odd probability 1/3 and even probability 2/3. An even sum requires matching parities, giving (3/4)(1/3)+(1/4)(2/3)=5/12. Alternatively, split the first wheel's half-disk into two elementary quarter-sectors: five of the resulting twelve equiprobable sector pairs are favorable. Both proposed routes are valid alternatives, and the unequal probabilities of the distinct first-wheel labels are correctly recognized.

figureEvidence.fact: On the first wheel, 3 occupies a semicircle while 1 and 2 each occupy a quarter-circle. The second wheel has three equal sectors labeled 4, 5, and 6.

audits.mathematicalReason: For fair, independent spins, the first wheel has two even and two odd sectors, while the second has one even and two odd sectors. Thus the even-sum probability is (2/4)(1/3)+(2/4)(2/3)=1/2. Equivalently, 2×1+2×2=6 of the 4×3=12 equiprobable sector pairs have matching parities. Enumeration and independent-event products followed by disjoint-case addition are both valid routes; neither must be used together with the other.

audits.mathematicalReason: Put the angle's vertex at (0,0) and P=(a,0), with a>0. Its rays have directions (1/2,√3/2) and (1/2,−√3/2). For every 0<t<a, choose Q=(t/2,√3t/2) and R=((a−t)/2,−√3(a−t)/2). Direct calculation gives PQ²=PR²=QR²=a²−at+t²>0, so each triangle is equilateral. Different t values give different unlabeled pairs of boundary vertices because each triangle has exactly one vertex on each ray. This proves an infinite family without needing to classify same-ray cases. Equivalently, a suitable 60° rotation about P maps a whole segment of one ray onto a segment of the other, validating the rotation route as well.

figureEvidence.fact: The figure shows two rays with a common vertex and P on the interior bisector, to the right of that vertex. The rays extend indefinitely, so their available points are not restricted to a finite boundary segment.

audits.mathematicalReason: Since F is a midpoint, AF=1 and AB=2. Right triangle ABF therefore has BF=√5 and area 1. Its altitude from A to BF is AG=2/√5. Matching the reassembled pieces identifies YZ with AG; this uses corresponding edges, not measured proportions in the sketch. Reassembly preserves area 4, so XY=4/(2/√5)=2√5 and XY/YZ=5. The alternative similarity route is also valid: triangles AFG and BFA are similar, giving AG/AB=AF/BF and the same altitude. The proposed area, Pythagorean, congruence-support, and alternative-route scopes are defensible.

figureEvidence.fact: In the square, F lies on AD, E lies on BC, and AG meets BF perpendicularly. The cuts form triangles ABG, AFG, and ECD together with parallelogram BFDE. In the reassembly, triangle AFG occupies the lower corner with its right angle at Z, and its edge AG corresponds to the rectangle's base YZ.
